title: Eagle Colorado Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Eagle wells have a 160-foot median depth, with fractured bedrock, variable siting conditions, and finished-well costs of $16,400-$28,000.
h1: What Eagle Colorado Wells Are Like
intro_html:
Buying land near Eagle means treating the well record as part of the property investigation. Within five miles of Eagle, Colorado DWR records show 418 permitted wells. Of those, 207 are recorded as constructed, 231 report a total depth, and 89 report a pump yield.

Most permits identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. That matters in mountain ground: two nearby lots can have different drilling results, water levels, and construction needs. Records from Gypsum, Wolcott, Edwards, Dotsero, Fulford, and Avon can provide useful regional context, but they do not replace a site-specific well investigation.

sections.heading: Eagle well depths reflect fractured mountain ground
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Eagle is 160 feet. The middle half runs from 52 to 268 feet, so a bid based only on the median may not cover the full range of ordinary results. The 90th percentile is 380 feet, and the deepest recorded well is 700 feet.

Depths are spread across the area: 44% are under 100 feet, 38% fall between 100 and 300 feet, 17% fall between 300 and 600 feet, and 1% are deeper than 600 feet. The permit records identify fractured bedrock, including granite and gneiss, on 402 wells. Fractures control where water is found, so the driller's experience with the immediate ridge, valley, or subdivision matters.

sections.heading: Reported Eagle well yields are generally strong, but verify the test
sections.html:
The reported yield median is 15.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 14.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Among the 89 wells reporting a pump yield, 72% report more than 15 gallons per minute, while 24% report between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Only 1% report under 1 gallon per minute, and 3% report between 1 and 5 gallons per minute.

Those figures describe reported well tests, not a guarantee for an unbuilt lot. Ask for the actual completion report, test duration, pump setting, and recovery information. A strong short-term yield can still require storage and careful pump sizing. An exempt household-use well is generally limited to 35 gallons per minute under Colorado rules, and the permit's allowed use still controls.

sections.heading: The Eagle water-level record is limited, not a trend line
sections.html:
Only 22 wells in the local records report a static water level. Their median depth to water is 94 feet, with the middle half from 26 to 163 feet. That gives a useful planning range for pump installation, casing, and electrical work, but it is not enough to establish a water-table trend for Eagle.

The records do not provide a water-level-by-decade series here, so they do not show whether groundwater is dropping over time. Static level also changes with season, weather, nearby pumping, and the time allowed for a well to recover. Before buying, request the well construction report and any recent water-level or production information. A driller should evaluate the proposed lot rather than apply the local median mechanically.

sections.heading: Eagle's permit history points to established local drilling experience
sections.html:
Permitting increased through the late twentieth century, with 143 permits in the 1990s and 68 in the 2000s. The records include 41 permits in the 2010s, 15 in the 2020s, and the newest permit year is 2025. Older records are concentrated in domestic and household use, which accounts for 56% of the local permits. Monitoring wells account for 24%.

The most frequently listed drillers are Golden Eagle Drilling Corporation, with 115 records; Steve Shelton Drilling, Inc., with 46; and Shelton Drilling Corporation, with 32. These names show who appears most often in the permit history, not who is available or best for a new project. Check current licensing, insurance, references, and proposed testing before hiring.

sections.heading: What drilling a new Eagle well can cost
sections.html:
In Eagle's fractured mountain bedrock, the drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the local median depth of 160 feet, the drilled hole works out to about $10,400 to $16,000. A finished well, including the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work, is estimated at about $16,400 to $28,000.

That is a planning range, not a fixed quote. The estimate can change with depth, access, casing and grout requirements, water testing, power distance, trench conditions, and whether the hole must be deepened or abandoned. Get the bid in writing and ask what happens if the hole is dry, produces too little water, or encounters unstable rock. A median-depth allowance should not be treated as a guaranteed maximum.

sections.heading: Check environmental sites, septic separation, and buildability
sections.html:
Mapped environmental records within about ten miles include 19 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 15 historic mine features, and 7 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These sites do not prove contamination on a particular parcel, but they justify a records search and water testing before closing. Ask about metals, bacteria, PFAS, and other tests recommended for the property's setting and well construction.

Low-yield and dry-hole risk remains possible in fractured rock even when nearby wells look productive. Confirm the proposed well location can meet Colorado setbacks from septic systems, property lines, and other sources of contamination. Mountain access, slope, drilling staging, driveway work, electrical service, and a septic design can affect the project as much as the hole itself. Have the well, septic, and house locations reviewed together.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Eagle, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within five miles of Eagle is 160 feet. The middle half runs from 52 to 268 feet, while the 90th percentile is 380 feet. The deepest recorded well is 700 feet. Because most permits identify fractured mountain bedrock, depth can vary significantly between nearby properties.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Eagle, Colorado?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 160-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $10,400 to $16,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work is estimated at $16,400 to $28,000. A difficult site or deeper hole can cost more.

faq.q: How much water do Eagle Colorado wells produce?
faq.a: Among 89 local wells reporting a pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 14.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Reported yields are above 15 gallons per minute for 72% of those wells. These are records, not a promise for a new lot, so require a documented test.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Eagle, Colorado?
faq.a: Well water is not automatically safe because it comes from a private well. Local records identify 19 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 15 historic mine features, and 7 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about ten miles. Test the specific well, including bacteria and site-appropriate contaminants, before using it for drinking.

faq.q: Are Eagle Colorado wells running out of water?
faq.a: The available records do not establish a declining water table. Only 22 wells report static water levels, with a median depth to water of 94 feet and a middle half from 26 to 163 feet. That sample is too limited for a trend. Review the individual well history, pumping test, and seasonal conditions before buying.
